For our analysis below, we include the entirety of the liabilities for the Dutch and French life insurance markets (excluding index-linked). In Germany we believe that only a modest slice of the market pursues tight hedging strategies. To capture this behaviour, about 25% of the total liabilities have been modelled for Germany, representing the portion of the industry we believe is most active in hedging interest rate risk. While we treat the Dutch and German liabilities as fixed, in France, we allow for the variable nature of the Eurofonds product, given that these contracts include a large profit-sharing element. This means that for these contracts current interest rates are used to both project and discount liabilities, giving a strongly offsetting effect and significantly reducing the DV01 compared to simply shifting the discount curve alone. Estimated changes to liabilities risk: With a very limited difference between the current and upcoming discount curves (Figure 1), the switch creates virtually no change to insurers’ outright DV01 risk (see Figure 6). However, changes in the mechanics of the extrapolation significantly shift key-point risk away from 20y, which sees a drop of EUR624mn DV01, in favour of other parts of the yield curve – mainly 10y, 15y, 25y and 30y. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 Executive summary U.S. potential growth is increasingly shaped by two opposing structural forces: immigration controls that reduce labor supply and productivity gains—potentially AI driven—that lift output per worker. Population dynamics have flipped sharply. After a surge in immigration lifted population estimates in early 2025, new Census data for January 2026 show that net international migration has slowed dramatically, cutting annual population growth roughly in half. With net international migration now falling from 2.7mn to 1.3mn and expected to slow further to 312,000, the U.S. is experiencing the sharpest slowdown in population inflows since the pandemic. Because immigrants tend to be younger, have higher participation rates, and work more hours, this decline materially reduces the capacity for hours worked, a key input to potential GDP. Trend hours worked are already weakening. The post pandemic rebound in hours – fueled by strong immigration – contributed over 1pp to potential growth in 2022–23. But with immigration slowing, that contribution has dropped to roughly 0.6pp presently, returning total hours to its pre COVID pace. Based on Census projections, trend hours could slow by another 40bp, and potentially more if the labor force shifts toward lower participation native born workers. Potential growth is decelerating. Rising AI adoption threatens enterprise software/SaaS models like SAP , while hardware and semiconductor names like ASML benefit. Divergence in equity market performance supports this: SAP shares fell ~40% YoY while ASML shares rose ~75%. EU credit markets show similar dispersion, with YTD spread moves in EU HY Tech becoming more divergent this year compared to last year, led by widening in higher disruption risk software names. This has narrowed the gap with the Bank Agents 3.4% private sector pay settlements expected this year. Productivity growth may be on an uptrend. Respondents to the latest DMP Survey expected AI to increase their firms’ productivity by around 0.6% per year on average over the next three years. The MPC expects productivity growth to track around 1% in the medium-term. This would add to the level at which wage growth would remain target-consistent. Overall supply growth is expected to outpace the Bank's GDP projections, adding to spare capacity. Fiscal policy will weigh on the output gap. The MPC expects the combined effect of the announced measures to directly reduce CPI inflation by 0.5pp at its peak in Q2-2026, bringing CPI to 2% in that quarter. While this hasn't changed the Bank's judgement on second-round effects, the faster drop in CPI is expected to pull down on inflation expectations. The MPC noted that "the risk of greater inflation persistence is judged to have continued to diminish, in part due to the lower near- term outlook for inflation". Equally, despite fiscal policy measures announced in the Budget expected to add to GDP growth, the overall fiscal stance remains tight. In the MPC’s central projection, the fiscal stance weighs on the output gap by around one percentage point by the end of the three-year forecast period. For households living in large metropolitan areas or in the bottom income quintile, the combined cost of the down payment and first-year mortgage has risen from 90-120% of income in 2000 to 160-200% today. If consumers’ overall spending power grows at a normal pace, should we still n worry about a particular item being more expensive than usual? We think the answer is yes in the case of housing, especially owner-occupied housing, because it is different in two crucial respects. First, owner-occupied housing is the primary way that many households, especially low-income households, save and build wealth. Second, in the US, neighborhoods offering high-quality public schools and other public amenities are predominantly owner-occupied. As a result, being unable to afford a home in these communities also means higher barriers to good schools, good jobs, and social mobility. records.text: 3 Insights Information Classification: General About PriceStats PriceStats is a source of high frequency inflation information drawn from prices of over five million items sold by online retailers. The items include food, beverages, electronics, apparel, furniture, household products, prescription drugs and over-the-counter medicines. The prices are collated for all the countries we monitor to produce individual Country Inflation Series. Country Inflation Series detect changes in inflation trends with real-time data. We publish the indices with a lag of three business days; they are direct reflections of prices of real products on sale at online retailers in each country. Country Inflation Series are not seasonally adjusted and are not designed to match official data. There are, however, a number of reasons that suggest gold is likely to trade with a non-trivial premium for a while. First of all, such misalignments to fair value are a fairly common occurrence for gold in the last 30 years. Gold has been similarly misaligned for sustained periods of time in the early 90s, late 90s, mid-00s, early-to-mid 2010s, and then post-COVID, in both directions (Figure 8). What is more, the standard deviation of such misalignments is c. 15%, which translates into $4400 currently. Second, such deviations tend to be long-lasting. On our estimates, the half-life of such misalignments – in other words the time it takes to correct 50% of the gap to fair value – is about one year. This means that we are likely still in the very first innings of this phase. Third, from a statistical point of view there is nothing abnormal about a long period of fair value undershooting being followed by a potentially prolonged period of overshooting. If anything, this is how markets ought to operate in their endless quest for price discovery. Fourth, in our model the cumulative inflation of the post-COVID period is the prime driver of gold's price, with gains c.5% for every 1% increase in the level of US CPI, all else equal. records.text: Japan’s Escape from Deflation Source: Bloomberg FROM DEFLATION TO INFLATION Japan’s inflation journey over the last five years has been an epic story. After decades of low inflation or outright deflation, Japan has managed to revive inflation through a variety of structural and cyclical forces. As shown in Exhibit 1, inflation beg an with imported and supply side inflation. COVID era goods disruptions and, later, commodity and energy shocks lifted global input costs, while yen depreciation amplified import prices and firms’ pass through behavior shifted. In its post exit policy reset, the BoJ noted that earlier import cost pass through had waned, but services prices continued to rise moderately, supported in part by wage increases. Another factor supporting a continued inflationary dynamic is the change in import price pass through and the impact of FX on inflation. The BoJ’s latest Outlook for Economic Activity and Prices notes that exchange rate changes now tend to affect consumer prices more than in the past. This reflects not only higher import penetration but also stronger “secondary spillover effects” tied to more active wage and price setting. Thus, what broke the deflationary trap was the combination of (i) a large and persistent imported cost shocks and (ii) corporate and labor market conditions that finally made pass through socially and politically feasible. records.text: The Summary of Opinions from the January 22–23 Monetary Policy Meeting indicates that considerable time was devoted not only to discussing further rate hike decisions but also to addressing the sharp rise in long-end JGB yields and how the Bank of Japan might respond. In line with Governor Ueda’s remarks at the post-MPM press conference, the SoP also contains comments suggesting that the BoJ could respond flexibly under “exceptional” circumstances. Nevertheless, the specific triggers that would prompt the BoJ to intervene in the bond market remain unclear. After the start of 2026, the 30‑year JGB yield repeatedly reached new historical highs, and amid rising fiscal concerns, long‑end JGBs sold off sharply—up 10.0bp on January 19 and 20.3bp (compound yields) on January 20. Even under these conditions, the BoJ chose not to intervene in the bond market. This suggests that (1) the absolute level of yields and (2) the magnitude of a single‑day yield increase are unlikely to serve as triggers for BoJ intervention. The BoJ has consistently noted that movements in short‑ to medium‑term rates have a relatively larger impact on economic activity and prices. records.text: Global Credit Strategy2 February 2026 ab 2 AI disruption will have a varying impact on default rates across markets We took two different approaches to estimate the potential rise in default rates in a fast, severe AI disruption scenario: [1] use historical sector-level default rates during stress periods (~25%) and apply this to the estimated share of each market at high disruption risk and [2] (1) break out the AI disruption risk exposure into three rating buckets and map these to historical transition matrices in higher default environments, assigning annual default rates of 5%, 10%, and 30% to each bucket. Across both of these methodologies, we project incremental default rates of 1-3% for US HY, 4-6% for US LL, 7.5-8.5% for US PC, 1-2.5% for EU HY, and 4-6% for EU LL, ceteris paribus. We find that HY markets have lower projected default rates due to their higher quality composition in high disruption risk names, but this composition mix shifts lower in quality when moving to LL and PC. Implied market-wide default rates would be more severe, which we estimate at 2-4% for US HY, 6-8% for US LL, 12-13% for US PC, 2-3% for EU HY, and 6-8% for EU LL. (It compares sample-based payroll growth to the birth-death estimate described above, to “exploit the .. relationship between the … sample-based ratio of employment change … and the actual birth-death input values derived from lagged QCEW data….”1 ) In the January payroll data, they will apply this method to post-benchmark months—the estimates since March 2025. The effect is likely to be noticeable but small relative to the overall benchmark revision. Slowing payrolls probably feed through into a slightly larger drag or smaller add from the net birth-death adjustment. The net birth-death adjustment is not usually revised much during the benchmark revision: the median revision, without regard to sign, of the last 20 years has been 11k per month. Omitting the revisions of the GFC, the median without regard to sign has been 7k per month. The new method could improve on these errors, but the overall impact on payrolls is likely small as revisions to the net birth-death estimates tend to be small. The BLS made the same alteration in estimating April-October 2024 post-benchmark months. Beyond that, longer-term upside in this ratio is likely more dependent on productivity gains accruing to equities amid a strong earnings cycle. The TGA remains an important variable to watch for the near-term liquidity set-up as well. Alongside this backdrop, we think it makes sense that the market is clearly rewarding stocks with high capex-to-sales ratios. This has been a dominant trend in the Tech, Communication Services and Materials sectors amid the massive AI investment cycle/data center build-out. It has been less evident in the Industrials sector where end market demand (ex-AI) has largely been softer for the past several years amid a persistent sub-50 ISM cycle. That could now change in 2026 as re-shoring gains more traction and we see a broadening of industrial production gains beyond the mega trends that have been dominant over the past several years. All in all, we think the market is signaling that capital spending today is likely to lead to productivity gains going forward (see our/our TMT colleagues' work on AI-related productivity gains). The aforementioned policy tailwinds should further support this dynamic and help to drive a broadening both in terms of capex itself and in terms of the sectors/industries that are rewarded for such spending.

records.text: M Idea 2 Once a year, the BLS benchmarks its sample-based payrolls estimate to the (almost) complete count of payrolls that unemployment-tax records provide in the QCEW. Until that benchmark, the BLS has to make assumptions about net changes in payrolls due to business openings (‘births’) and business closings (‘deaths’). They use QCEW data to extrapolate past employment changes due to births and deaths into post-benchmark payrolls. Our preview of the January employment report: "Employment Report Preview: Stabilizing labor market, with temporary private payrolls spike" What is the net birth-death adjustment? The payroll survey directly covers about ¼ of nonfarm payroll employees in the US. It cannot pick up new business formation and the payrolls attached to them. And it cannot count the payrolls at businesses that are part of the payrolls sample but do not respond. These payroll changes from nonrespondents, businesses births, and businesses deaths are invisible to the survey. The net birth/death model attempts to fix for those, in a two step process. First, from the payroll estimate, the BLS assumes that businesses’ nonresponses and zeros on payrolls, even though they might be business deaths, are offset by the employment at business births. It imputes the employment due to business births from the business deaths. Then, it looks at the complete, QCEW employment count to assess the accuracy of that assumption. We also see scope that this investor group may be diversifying its USD fixed income holdings away from a heavy UST skewed portfolio, with corporates and mortgages providin g spread support, especially if our expected bear steepening materializes. For the moment, Treasury and Bessent have managed a tricky issuance environment well, something that will become more difficult as deficits grow and possible tariff refunds remains a real threat to government cashflows. For the moment, Treasury has used the Fed’s buying power tailwind to focus its issuance, a backdrop that will be increasingly harder as the Fed’s overall goal of reducing the balance sheet in aggregate may take hold w ith new Fed management. records.text: 2026 has started with a clang Since the beginning of 2025, both base and precious metals have staged a sharp and broad- based rally, pushing several complexes toward, or through, record highs. For context, since January 1, 2025, silver is up more than 150% (even after the recent sharp selloff), tin 60%, gold 80%, copper 50%, and aluminum 20% (Figure 1). The move has occurred against a backdrop of shifting preferences for foreign reserve managers, easing financial conditions, concerns regarding US dollar debasement and global de-dollarization, and tentative signs of a global growth acceleration, even if there has been retracement in recent days. It raises questions about whether the repricing reflects cyclical fundamentals, financial positioning, or a deeper macro signal. This repricing of base and precious metals could be consequential for realized inflation and markets. FIGURE 1. records.text: slowdown in hours worked? If the prior technology innovation cycle is any guide, productivity growth could rise by more than trend hours slows. After all, productivity growth accelerated by 100-150bp per year during the productivity boom of the 1990s. Are we seeing that now? No, not yet. The upcoming benchmark revisions to employment will be a key factor. If employment growth is revised sharply lower, it would indicate stronger productivity gains and could reveal a different underlying trend. For now, we retain our outlook for further deceleration in potential growth across our forecast horizon in 2026-27. We think it plausible that potential growth could slip back below 2.0%, or about where it fluctuated after the financial crisis and before the pandemic. Whether it ultimately does will depend on whether immigration controls are maintained and whether the corporate sector can adopt AI and other cost-saving measures more rapidly than we estimate. Stay tuned.

That update resulted in the unemployment rate being revised up by one-tenth in February, May, and July, and revised down in November. Given this precedent, revisions to the Establishment survey seasonal factors may also cluster in particular months, especially around turning points such as June/September (summer transitions) or December/January (holiday season) where post-pandemic changes (like more online shopping requiring fewer workers hired during a more spread- out holiday season) caused historical seasonal patterns to shift. Is residual seasonality still at play in January? We have fielded some questions on the potential for residual seasonality to boost employment in January. Post pandemic, January has lower layoffs after the holiday season, so, seasonal factors in January should be less favorable now. Seasonal factors have been gradually catching up to this. Recent data show the adjustment has likely largely caught up. Indeed, in 2024, January job growth actually came in below the average pace for the rest of the year, and in 2025, while still somewhat elevated, the January gain was smaller than in 2023 (Exhibit 5), indicating diminishing residual seasonality. So, we don’t think residual seasonality will provide a significant boost to January payrolls in 2026. Will the HH survey data also be revised in the Jan report? records.text: The Growing Challenge of Housing Affordability The cost of living has become a major political theme in recent years. This might seem surprising at first because real disposable income, both in aggregate and for each income quintile, returned a while ago to roughly its pre-pandemic trend (Exhibit 1). But housing, particularly owner-occupied housing, continues to present a major affordability challenge, especially for low-income families. For renters, housing costs are high by historical standards. Exhibit 2 shows that rent currently amounts to 32% of the average renter’s household income. This is not meaningfully different from the share in the 2010s but somewhat higher than the 27% share that prevailed in the 1980s and 1990s. Another “upside surprise” for January core CPI? January core CPI has surprised to the upside vs. Bloomberg consensus expectations in 14 of the last fifteen years. Even recent February CPI prints have been strong. Additionally, outside the covid years of 2020 and 2021, core PCE in 1Q each year has been stronger than the rest of the year – suggesting some residual seasonality risks. These residual seasonality risks have been further heightened in the post pandemic years, where the seasonal adjustments likely do not fully account for annual front-loading of price resets. We also see near-term fiscal policy tailwinds, stimulative monetary policy, stimulative financial conditions, and emerging evidence that AI is starting to scale into the economy and driving a productivity boom – all adding to upward pressure on yields. Overall, we see upside risks to all – labor markets data, growth, and also inflation – making for an attractive period to stay positioned for higher yields inn the coming few weeks. Why? The MPC at large has started to put more weight on risk management considerations, owing to the fragile labour market and projected drop in CPI to 2% by spring. Bottom line, the Bank thinks that price dynamics are likely to return to more 'normal' levels in the coming years as wage bargaining power remains tepid. The MPC is looking at productivity growth and import prices to justify above 3% wage settlements. While the MPC has put more stock on the absolute level wage settlements as a measure for target-consistency in the past, it has expanded its framework to include import prices, labour productivity, and firms' margins. With the MPC now assuming import price inflation of 1%, import intensity of 25%, 0% margins contribution, and 1% productivity growth, the Bank now thinks target consistent wage growth is likely closer to 3.25% - a slight upgrade from before. With the Census Bureau now projecting population growth of 0.5%, versus nearly 1.0% annual growth in 2023-2025, trend hours are set to slow further. records.text: Increased uncertainty has not tilted the ECB's balance of risks to the downside. The assessment of risks in the monetary policy statement remained broadly unchanged from December. We believe the ECB needs more evidence of a materialisation of any of the risks before it may change its language. As President Lagarde noted today, a single below target inflation print is not enough to ask for a change in policy. The projected return to inflation over the medium term is what is important. And here the risks clearly cloud the outlook. So it's wait and see. Observe gradual shifting: Any travel from here will be slow and gradual, informed by incoming data. If data confirms our view of the economy, featuring further disinflation (see here), moderating wage growth, a further appreciation of the euro, and GDP growth significantly below the ECB's expectations (see Exhibit 4below), the Council's balance of risks will start to shift to the downside. Looking at the accounts, there is a small group of Council members currently seeing inflation risks as skewed to the downside. An even smaller group sees the skew going the other way. More importantly, the majority of the Council is sitting on the fence here. Data coming our way would likely mean that some governors currently sitting in the neutral camp would start emphasizing downside risk. However, the preliminary estimate of the 2025 benchmark revision that will be reported this week remained very large: the payrolls sampling itself is a much larger source of error than the net birth-death adjustment. In the 12 months through March 2025, the net birth-death adjustment, totalled across all the months, added 263k less than in the prior year. The April-October months, where the new method was applied, accounted for the entire difference. Compared to currently reported payrolls that is a large piece of the slowing in the year March 2025. Payroll growth is currently reported as slowing by 569k over the full period relative to a year earlier. (Payrolls rose 2359k in the 12 months through March 2024 and 1790k in the 12 months through March 2025---a 569k difference.) But if the preliminary estimate of the benchmark revision is correct, the slowdown over that period will be 911k greater, or 1.48 million slower payroll growth than in the year earlier. The contribution of the net birth-death adjustment to the slowdown is relatively small. The incorporation of payroll sample data to the net birth-death adjustment may amplify accelerations and decelerations in payrolls. It also may increase volatility. Our underlying view of the UK economy has not changed. For one, we continue to think that the Bank is somewhat behind the curve on the cutting cycle and that this may be deliberate policy choice. Bank of England Delivering a dovish hold The MPC held Bank Rate at 3.75% at its February meeting with a 5-4 vote split. The tone of the accompanying minutes was more dovish than expected. The updated forecast saw inflation and GDP revised down and unemployment revised up. • The MPC delivered a narrow 5-4 majority to hold Bank rate at 3.75%, with four members of the committee preferring a 25bp cut. • The forecast revisions bring the near-term outlook into line with our own expectations for data releases over the next six weeks. However, we think validation of the MPC's near-term forecast would be sufficient for there to be a majority to vote for a 25bp rate cut at the March meeting. This solidifies our conviction in our existing call for a March cut to 3.5%. • We retain our baseline that March will be the final cut of this cycle, leaving Bank rate at 3.5%, but we acknowledge that the more dovish tone of this meeting's minutes and worse labour market forecast increase the risk that another cut beyond March is needed. • More generally, the February MPR forecast showed: ° GDP was revised downwards in 2026, with the annual average forecast now 0.9% y/y, compared with 1.2% in November. Annual averages were little changed in other years, revised down 0.1pp to 1.4% in 2025 and 0.1pp to 1.5% in 2027, and revised up 0.1pp to 1.9% in 2028. ° The unemployment rate was revised up, now expected to peak at 5.3%

Strategy View: Biding Time The BoE won’t be rushed: The February BoE meeting could reveal some important updates on the outlook for wage growth (via the annual Agents’ pay survey, with early indications suggesting a drop in average pay settlements from 3.9% in 2025 to 3.5% in 2026) as well as a full assessment of the impact of fiscal policy decisions taken at the Budget. It is clear to us, however, that the BoE will not be rushed into its next decision. Indeed, since the last BoE meeting in December, the market has removed any chance of a cut at the 5 February meeting and reduced the chance of a cut in March – Figure 1. The market views April as most likely for the next cut, in line with the Citi view. This also fits neatly with the new, slower pace established at the December meeting of cutting at the third meeting since the last cut, compared with every other meeting for the first five cuts. records.text: 30 y swap spread remains attractive outright, but also as a hedge for our 1 s 30 s steepener view . “T-bill and chill” is alive…but the affordability push needed more: In November, the Treasury surprised investors by saying they were “preliminarily considering” an increase in coupon sizes. At the February refunding, the Treasury clarified that guidance by noting that an increase in coupons was going to be linked to “trends in structural demand” while also noting that there is a “growing demand for bills” in the same breath. There were also suggestions from the TBAC to increase bill issuance and focus on increasing coupon issuance in shorter tenors and intermediate maturities. All these references reinforce our structural view that the Treasury is likely to focus any incremental financing needs in bills (and front-end coupons) – i.e. T-bill and chill. However, the discussion at the February refunding is not overt enough for swap spreads to widen (see US rates: Two chances, one opportunity, dated 29 January), especially given that there are concerns that Fed chair nominee Kevin Warsh may look to shrink the Fed’s balance sheet (see US rates: Rates higher for longer, dated 20 January). We also note that insurers are allowed to choose between adopting the full extrapolation change on 30 January 2027 or scaling in the changes over a five-year period from 2027 to 2032. Given the negligible expected impact in total liability DV01, we expect the majority of insurers will adopt the full change in January 2027. USDINR had broadly moved higher over the past year largely in response to the tariff headwinds (we estimated USDINR fair value under 50% tariffs ~90-92 levels to offset the effects from tariffs) and portfolio outflows (given rich equity valuations at a time when growth was cooling). With US tariffs being lowered to 18%, we estimate USDINR fair value closer to 86.50-88 level now. India’s trade deal with the US encompasses USD 500bn of goods purchases, with no timeline outlined for this to be completed by. However, we note purchases may include US energy, and the deal is also predicated on India stopping it’s purchases of Russian oil. A full pivot away from Russian crude to US/Venezuela sources could add ~USD 40bn to India’s imports from the US (assuming USD 60/bbl oil price). On top of the existing ~USD 50bn/year goods imports from the US (in 2025), total annual US imports could rise to ~USD 90bn imports/year, making USD 500bn goods purchases feasible over a 5-6y horizon, similar to the 5-10y investment horizons seen in the US’ other trade deals with Japan and Korea. Even as tariff risks abate, we caution against complacency because key questions remain unanswered – namely how the Supreme Court rules regarding IEEPA and what will happen with the USMCA negotiations. Both outcomes are highly consequential for the future of supply chains and investment flows. In our latest global tariff publication, we examined the lagged trade data delayed by the US government shutdown. Nominal tariffs fell from 16% in September to 13% at year end, as import composition shifts and exclusions began to be realized. The effective tariff rate is even lower, hovering near 11%. The nominal versus effective tariff gap is explained almost entirely by fuel, gold, AI, and pharmaceuticals, where there are explicit tariff exclusions. Both nominal and effective tariff rates could move lower should the Supreme Court rule against IEEPA. Even though the Administration could replicate the tariff structure to a degree, such a ruling would likely further accelerate the transition from country to sector tariffs, as we have been arguing. The headlines around tariffs mask the interesting details that are starting to appear in the data – first is the shift in which countries the US directly imports from, but simultaneously not clear change in original production capacity for traded goods. To improve accuracy, the BLS temporarily adjusted the model from April through October 2024 by incorporating current sample-based employment growth, making the adjustment more responsive to current labor market conditions. With the release of the December 2025 jobs report, the BLS has announced that this current sample informed approach will be adopted permanently starting with the January 2026 employment report. What is our estimate for the Birth-Death model revision? Business formation has cooled materially from post pandemic highs, while closures and survival rates have risen amid tighter financial conditions and slower growth. The historically trained model likely overstates the job gains from net new businesses. Indeed, as seen in Exhibit 4, net establishment birth-death adjustment from the BLS’s Birth-Death model, despite slowing down in the last year continues to be above pre- pandemic levels. However, data on firm openings and closures from the Business Employment Dynamics (BED) Survey suggest that net establishment change is now running below its pre-pandemic levels. Even if the QCEW based revision to the more recent months happens only in 2027, a dovish argument could be made that it will almost inevitably be a modest downward revision. What is the Birth-Death model and why does BLS use it? The Establishment survey applies a Birth-Death model adjustment to account for net employment changes from new business formations (births) and closures (deaths) that are not yet captured in the monthly sample in the CES based Establishment survey for payrolls. This is because new firms enter the survey with a lag and failing firms can drop out quickly. This is intended to prevent undercounting in expansions and overcounting in downturns. To compensate for this unavoidable lag, the BLS adjusts its monthly employment estimates using a two-part procedure: first, it imputes continued employment to firms that have disappeared from the sample (offsetting missing job gains from births), and second, it applies a time series model trained on five years of historical QCEW microdata to estimate the residual net effect of business openings and closings. Interest Rate Derivatives Systematic strategies in rate volatility – lower implied but even lower realised We discuss how a range of simulated USD/ EUR/ GBP rate vol risk premia strategies that we have previously documented have performed over the past three months, and highlight vol market trends that have driven them. Summary • Short gamma has delivered exceptionally strong returns across maturities and markets, notably in the US, as historically low realised vol widened vol risk premium. Relative value in gamma sees little exploitable dislocation across the term structure and more opportunities cross markets. • Long-dated vega faced a persistent drawdown as bottom right implied vol declined, amplified by the absence of traditional positive carry components such as vol roll-up and gamma driven gains, in the current low realised vol environment. • Option triangles (forward vol) strategies stand out as an effective way to own long-term vol. records.text: European Rates Weekly 06 February 2026 Citi Research 2 The twist steepening in gilts owes to a dovish BoE vs political uncertainty. The chance of a BoE cut in March has increased, but we still think the MPC will be slow to reach its trough rate, which we estimate at 3%. The politics is a tough call, but we opt to stay long 30yr gilts vs Bunds thinking that a leadership challenge is still most likely after May. In the meantime, issuance – and the dovish BoE – are potentially supportive for gilts. At its meeting, the ECB said it was keeping an eye on FX, but euro appreciation seems far from being relevant anytime soon. Dovish BoE…. Let’s twist again. A dovish BoE combined with heightened political uncertainty led to a sharp twist steepening of the gilt curve on Thursday (see Figure 1). Greater chance for an earlier cut. The market has switched to March as most likely for the next cut vs April previously (see Figure 2). There were several catalysts: a) Stronger-than-expected appetite for back-to-back cuts, with a 5-4 vote to hold (vs Citi expectations for 7-2); b) A dovish shift in the projections with CPI at target from April, thanks to Budget energy measures, activity marked lower for 2026, and unemployment higher; c) A shift from Catherine Mann to say that developments have moved the “time for a cut in Bank Rate closer”. records.text: UK Economics and Rates 29 January 2026 Citi Research 7 Labour market data continues to be split. It remains difficult to get an accurate and convincing grasp as to the state of the UK labour market. The standout point of the latest release (see UK Economics: An Inconsequential Beat on Pay) was a beat in wages. This, however, comes with the usual caveats: public sector pay (which was 7.9% 3M/YoY) warrants discounted because of pronounced base effects; meanwhile. private pay (3.6% 3M/YoY) remains only just above inflation, with some sectors already seeing notable real-terms pay loss. Unemployment saw a small increase, with the 3M rate unchanged at 5.1% but the 1M rate stronger at 5.3%. On the quantities side of employment, though, the data is mixed: LFS was stronger than expected while payrolled employees was softer. Vacancies more or less moved sideways, but we remain down 8.6% YoY in December with the unemployed-to-vacancies still moving up. We think it is difficult to form a strong view off the recent, official data and await to see where pay lands once public- sector pay starts to stabilise. But survey data continues to point to wage pressure. Foremost amongst these is the Agent’s Pay Survey, which remains stubborn at +3 (scale of -5 to +5, with higher scores indicating strong growth), where it has been since October 2024. Th e percentiles have the advantage of making no assumptions about the shape of the distribution of the indicators, such as normality. Our use is aimed at being a simple way of ranking flow and positioning indicators relative to their own history. For all of the flow indicators within the Investment Climate, we calculate the percentiles based on the distribution of flows over the last five years using the daily aggregate time periods shown in the tables. Before calculating the percentiles, we constrain the 50 th percentile as equivalent to neutral. Flows above the 50 th percentile, therefore, are all positive and those below the 50th all represent selling of the market in question. A 100th percentile reading represents the strongest buying in five years; and a zero percentile equals the strongest selling. A reading in the 50th percentile would signal that net flows in the asset over the period are at zero. We use a simple colour coding scheme to highlight strong (top 20 th percentile) and weak (bottom 20th percentile) flows. The Fed began its rate- cutting cycle in September, and we see potential for that to be extended through 2026 by a new Fed chair, even as other central banks are pricing out further cuts. This creates a clearly supportive backdrop for gold via a weaker USD. The US administration has set out an array of fiscally stimulative policy measures over 2026 into the mid-terms, with fiscal deficits increasing, likely acceleration in monetary stimulus, the Fed ending QT (link) and rising capital spending while labour supply remains constrained. All these are likely to encourage investors to seek inflation hedges as the year progresses, which should continue to be supportive for gold. Central bank buying continued to be a significant support to gold prices in 2025. Absolute purchases declined 21% YoY in 2025 in ounce terms based on WGC data, but in USD value terms purchases rose 13% YoY and we note Q4-25 was the second highest USD purchasing period on record (after Q4-24). This highlights the continued desire by central banks to diversify away from US treasuries following the freezing of the Russian central bank’s treasury reserves in 20222 . We also highlight Tether (private, not covered), the world's largest stablecoin issuer, has emerged as the world's largest buyer of gold in Q3, ahead of global central banks. records.text: Does this mean that inflation markets should ignore the rise in industrial metals? Absolutely not. The risk is that there is some informational content in the sharp rally in industrial and precious metals that suggests strong demand for inflation protection not being executed directly in inflation markets. In this state of the world, inflation markets may be significantly underpricing upside risk premium. Indeed, that was a key concern we flagged at the start of the year in Are inflation markets calm or complacent? (January 5, 2026). To flush this out slightly more, while this publication has largely focused on industrial metals, precious metals have little-to-no direct/mechanical passthrough impact on US inflation, and yet, are often seen as an inflation hedge. And, one of the biggest stories of 2026 so far has been the extraordinary rise in gold and silver prices to all-time record highs (although that is retracing of late). Without overthinking it, when copper, silver, tin, gold, and aluminum are all rising rapidly to multi-year highs, the potential inflation risk seems apparent and the market should price a meaningful positive inflation risk premium. To project a precise price passthrough to 2yfwd3y or 5y5y would imply false precision and stability in the relationship, but even then, were 5y5y to even rise to near the post-COVID highs, that represents 20bp of upside. records.text: Marija Veitmane 3-February-2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Global Equity Strategy: Weekly Small Caps: A Story Still Missing a Spark Small Caps are often touted as the next leg of outperformance: they screen cheap and remain under-owned after years of lacklustre earnings. In theory, they should start to lead once profits recover. And indeed, they opened the year on a strong note as investors searched for alternatives to crowded and expensive Tech. However, we still see little evidence of an earnings-rebound in the Small-Cap space—making sustained outperformance this year unlikely. No earnings, no outperformance. To paraphrase The Beatles classic, “All You Need Is Love”, All Small Caps Need is Earnings ; and this has been our refrain for years. Small Caps have been trading at a substantial discount to their larger counterparts making them one of the favourite trades for contrarian investors. W e continue to believe that the valuation discount reflects weaker earnings potential and remains unlikely to reverse, especially at times of broader economic and earnings uncertainty. The question remains: Is 2026 different? Should Small Cap companies finally improve their profitability? Our analysis concludes that it is still too early to expect a turnaround in profitability. Catalyst.Metric: Metal price shock impact on CPI/PCE inflation

records.text: production come from the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas and the IMF. We estimate that a 10% metal price shock raises headline CPI inflation by 0.2pp (18bp) after 12 months, and the effect accumulates to about 0.3pp at 24 months after the shock. For core CPI, the effects are a bit smaller, with inflation rising 0.1pp (7bp) after 12 months, and peaking at 0.2pp (18bp) at the two-year mark. These results are similar for the PCE price index, and robust to using the different measures of metal prices and industrial production listed above. A 10% persistent metal price shock raises headline CPI by 0.3pp over two years, while core CPI rises by about 0.2pp over the same period. Our estimates are broadly consistent with the findings in a recent IMF Working Paper by Miranda-Pinto et al. (2024). Using a balanced panel of 39 countries, they estimate that a 10% copper price increase would lift headline and core CPI inflation by about 0.2 pp within a year on average, and the effects grow to ~0.5 pp for headline CPI, and 0.3pp for core CPI at about 24 months. These estimates illustrate that metals do eventually impart measurable inflationary influence, provided the shock is persistent, and that the effects peak after roughly 24 months, likely reflecting contracts renegotiated, menu prices changed, and possibly wage adjustments in affected industries. 3 February 2026 7 Barclays | Thinking Macro

Our understanding of MPC communication since the last meeting is renewed focus on the management of the balance of risk versus the cost of risk. By this, we believe that the committee has become more receptive to the reality that an overly restrictive rate may lead to CPI missing in the medium term, but that the costs of misjudging this event, and cutting too far or too fast, is more damaging. As such, we still view the committee as bifurcated but believe the reasons to remain on hold have changed in subtle, but important, ways. The central theme of MPC communication has been the exogenous risks for UK monetary policy. We saw this iterated by Governor Bailey, Ms. Greene and Professor Taylor, although their conclusions were varied. As a point of agreement, all three speakers emphasised that Britain’s position as an open economy left it exposed to exogenous factors that are difficult to compensate for in the making of monetary policy. For Ms. Greene,3 this imparts a clear policy risk that necessitates the need for what can be called “policy space” —or the need to have redundancy in policymaking to respond to external shocks. It’s clear that the prior administration also intended to drive nominal growth higher, but with a much different strategy of growing population via immigration and then using heavy government subsidies directed at consumers to stimulate real demand and inflation. The argument against this strategy is that this mix of growth is likely to lead to more inflation and less real growth as it’s less focused on stimulating sustained productivity gains in the private sector. It also crowds out much of the middle class and smaller businesses that are adversely impacted by the higher inflation and don’t necessarily have the offsets to help them compete with the mega caps that have scale. It appears that the current administration is focused on driving a more sustained mix of real growth and inflation by rebalancing the economy on three different planes, simultaneously: • Current/trade accounts: the “international” imbalance ° Policy: tariffs/weaker USD • Over-consumption vs. under-investment: the “domestic” imbalance ° Policy: tariffs/weaker USD and OBBBA tax incentives for capex • The k-economy: the “inequality” imbalance for corporates and consumers ° Policy: immigration enforcement and de-regulation The end goal of these policies is the same—to grow out of the debt problem. When winter weather intervened, prices spiked in January on stronger-than-expected storage draws and a colder weather forecast. Short covering extended the rally beyond what would have otherwise been the case. We don’t believe this is reason to panic, though lower-than-expected end-of- winter storage levels will have an impact on the balance for 2026 (TTF spikes by 30% – like last year, no need for panic, 16 January). Figure 3 shows we expect EU gas stocks to deplete to 26% by 31 March. That implies a strong injection season is needed to start next winter around 90%, see Figure 4 (while this isn’t a hard target anymore, we expect one of the lessons from this winter will be not to start winter much below 90%). Given another year of likely strong LNG supply increases (Figures 6, 7), we think this is possible without needing significant price spikes. We do, of course, need economic incentives to store gas (Figure 5). Further upside depends on weather: The balance of winter provides upside risk given relatively low stocks. However, this needs a catalyst (another cold snap for example); without that, we expect the market to trend down. records.text: fts toward lower participation native born workers. Potential growth is decelerating. We estimate U.S. potential growth has already slipped from 3.0% in 2022 to 2.3% currently, with risks of falling below 2% in 2026 if immigration controls persist. Productivity is the counterweight. Recent gains in output per hour—supported by automation, efficiency pressures, and early AI adoption—offer some offset. However, the current four quarter productivity trend near 1.9% remains close to our longer run estimate and has not yet demonstrated a sustained break higher. It is too early to conclude that an AI driven productivity boom will compensate for slowing labor force growth, but it certainly could. It could fully compensate for lower capacity in total hours, or it could make any slowdown in potential growth short-lived Bottom line: With immigration slowing sharply and productivity gains not yet accelerating meaningfully, the U.S. appears headed toward a period of slower potential GDP growth, with the balance of risks tilting lower for 2026–27. Whether potential growth stabilizes or declines further will depend on (1) how restrictive immigration policies remain and (2) how quickly firms adopt AI and other labor saving technologies.

Hence, population control adjustments that change the size of the population will lead to changes in the reported levels of the population, labor force, employment, and unemployment, but not the ratios themselves (there is some feed-through from new population estimates to the ratios if the new population estimates include substantially different shares of demographic groups, but these shifts are usually small on the order of tenths of a percent). This is why we – and the Federal Reserve – pay greater attention to the ratios more than level changes in recent years when volatility in immigration flows have caused larger-than-normal changes in population estimates. When looking at other components of the January 2025 adjustments, they also had immigration overtones. The upward adjustment to the population fell disproportionately on Asians and Hispanics. The increase for Whites, while sizable, mainly reflected growth in the Hispanic population (since people of Hispanic or Latino ethnicity may be of any race according to Census Bureau definitions). By age, most of the increase occurred among people under age 55, with comparatively small effects for those 55 and older.

Less immigration to reduce capacity for hours worked A year ago we released our initial take on what effect restrictive immigration policies would have on the US economy (see Immigration and the macroeconomy, 20 February 2025). Our key findings were 1) the surge in immigration helped the US economy to "soft land" following a period of high inflation as the economy exited the pandemic, 2) reduced immigration could mean slow employment growth coincides with a low unemployment rate, and 3) potential growth could slow since less immigration implies slower growth in the labor force and capacity for hours worked. Whether this ultimately meant slower potential growth would depend on changes in productivity. We were confident in our thinking that growth in trend hours would slow, but that is only part of the story. Immigration controls push potential growth lower while productivity gains push potential growth higher. We leaned in the direction of thinking immigration would weigh on growth in trend hours before AI investment could push productivity higher, but the tug-of-war will ultimately be decided by the data. records.text: US Economic Viewpoint | 05 February 2026 3 Given the wide array of factors impacting each of these updates, below we answer some frequently asked client questions on each topic. We also detail out our estimate for the expected size of the revisions, along with implications for the labor market and the Fed. FAQs: QCEW-based benchmark revisions What is the QCEW? Is it better than the payroll survey? The QCEW data represent approximately 95% of total employment and are compiled from state level unemployment insurance data that nearly all employers are required to file. This dataset is more accurate for estimating nonfarm payrolls than the Establishment survey, which samples about 120k businesses and government agencies (covering one-third of payroll employment) in the CES (Current Employment Statistics) survey. But the problem is the QCEW data are published with a lag of about five months, while the payroll data are published in a timelier manner at a monthly frequency. What is the annual QCEW based benchmark revision? Each year with the release of the January employment report, the Establishment survey data are benchmarked by the BLS to reflect more complete counts of employment from the QCEW. Hence in February of this year along with the release of the January employment report, the payroll data from April 2024 to December 2025 will be subject to a benchmark revision by the BLS. This year, however, the agency has announced that the updated population controls will instead be introduced with the February jobs report which will be released in March, likely reflecting delays stemming from last year’s shutdown. These revisions will apply only on a go forward basis, which means there will be level shifts in measures such as household employment, unemployment, and the labor force in February. As a result, monthly changes in these variables for February should be interpreted with caution. We expect the population update to produce downward revisions. Census Bureau estimates for July 2024 to July 2025 show U.S. population growth running at roughly half the prior year’s pace due to lower net migration. So, we expect a reduction in the labor force and household employment & unemployment levels in February.

records.text: M Idea 4 US population growth slows sharply on less net international migration The Census Bureau recently released its updated population estimates that will be reflected in the Current Population Survey (CPS, or Household Survey). Normally the Census Bureau releases its population estimates in December, for incorporation into the January Household Survey Data. Due to the federal government shutdown in 4Q 2025, the release was delayed until January 21, 2026. Background on population controls The Census Bureau produces independent population estimates, known as "population controls." These controls are used to weight the Current Population Survey (CPS) with the aim of ensuring that the survey results accurately reflect the size and demographic makeup of the civilian noninstitutional population age 16 and older. Because the underlying population changes over time, these controls are updated every year and take effect with the release of January employment data, which is released on Friday, February 6. Each year, the Census Bureau revises its population estimates to incorporate the latest information on births, deaths, and migration, as well as any improvements in its estimation methods. For January 2025, the updated population controls were based on the Bureau’s Vintage 2024 estimates, which themselves draw on a blended population base established after the 2020 Census. One piece of the structural picture is becoming clearer: Growth in trend hours is slowing Instead, we focus our remarks on the potential structural effects of immigration controls and, in particular, their read through to potential growth. According to national income and product account identities, potential GDP growth is the sum of growth in trend hours worked in the nonfarm business sector and growth in trend output per hour in the nonfarm business sector, or productivity. Hours worked in the nonfarm business sector is the combination of employment, labor force participation, and the work week. After all, total hours worked in the economy is the product of three ingredients: how many people are willing to work (participation), how many people hold jobs (employment), and how many hours each employed person works (the average workweek). Together, they define trend labor input and determine how much labor the economy can supply under "normal" or sustainable conditions. Immigration controls that reduce net international migration can reduce trend hours directly by slowing the rate of population growth and, in turn, the working age population. In addition, fewer immigrants can change the composition of the labor force since the average foreign-born worker is of younger age than the domestic-born labor force and participates in the workforce at a higher rate. And for good reason: key economic data for January (released in February) has tended to surprise to the upside. We think February 2026 will be no different. We see fundamental and seasonal tailwinds aligning for a strong US economy and higher UST yields in the coming weeks, starting with nonfarm payrolls on 6 February (see our preview here). We also tend to see upside surprises in core CPI with 14 of the last 15 years delivering this result. Notably, the UST curve tends to bear flatten in the early weeks of February. records.text: n the extrapolation (known as the Last Liquid Point or LLP) is the 20y swap rate versus 6-month Euribor. Beyond this point the discount curve gradually converges towards the Ultimate Forward Rate (UFR), currently set at 3.3%. Full convergence to the UFR occurs by year 60. This means insurers have a very significant key-point risk at the 20y but no market risk beyond this maturity, with key-point risk measuring the impact of shifting only a specific point or segment of the curve. The mechanics of SW method extrapolation also leave insurers with a counterintuitive long rates exposure at the 15y point (i.e. benefitting from a move lower in yields at this point). Under the Alternative Method, the extrapolation still converges to the UFR and still has 20y as the LLP (although this will now be called the First Smoothing Point). However, rather than using the 20y swap as the starting point for the extrapolation, it uses something called the Last Liquid Forward Rate (LLFR). The LLFR uses a combination of forward swap rates from 15y to 50y, weighted by the traded swap volume at the different pillar points on the curve (i.e. 20y, 25y, 30y, 40y and 50y). KEY MESSAGES Changes to the way European insurers model long- term interest-rate risk are set to prompt meaningful changes to hedging strategies from January 2027. Nor did the SOP provide new insights regarding the indicators used to assess the Bank’s key concept of the “underlying inflation rate.” Separately from the MPM discussions, a working paper1 published by BoJ staff on Friday presented a new estimate of Japan’s “trend inflation rate,” using a statistical technique known as Trend-Cycle BVAR Decomposition. The model, which incorporates structural factors such as labor supply and productivity along with inflation expectations that the Bank has consistently emphasized, estimates that Japan’s trend inflation rate has recently been fluctuating around 2%. This new estimate could influence the Bank’s communication on the future rate hike path and the terminal rate. records.text: Japan FX 02 February 2026 Citi Research 4 Reduction in consumption tax on food The coalition documents signed by the LDP and the JIP ahead of the current election campaign promote a policy of cutting the consumption tax on food to zero for two years. However, while the JIP has made this an official pledge, the LDP has said only that it will push forward with efforts to consider the policy in a National Council (a cross-party council). As this is also requested by the US, there is little doubt defense spending will grow further over time. Given PM Takaichi’s her emphasis on national security, the administration might find funding it to be an important issue. Thus, even if the ruling coalition wins the election, we do not consider a cut in the consumption tax on food (decline in tax revenue of around ¥5trn annually) to be certain. Should the LDP win a majority in its own right, we think the LDP will not dissolve its coalition with the JIP because it will want to maintain its numbers in the Upper House as well. However, in this case the political negotiating power of the JIP would be somewhat diminished. In our view, the greater the number of seats gained in the election by the LDP under PM Takaichi, the less likely the cut to the consumption tax on food is to go ahead. records.text: 023, hiring rate and domestic demand are uncorrelated Source: BEA, BLS, Haver Analytics, Deutsche Bank Research Source: BEA, BLS, Haver Analytics, Deutsche Bank Research This divergence has had at least two significant implications for the economy. First, weaker hiring, which manifested in soft payrolls and a modest rise in labor market slack, was the primary reason the Fed cut rates by 175bps over the past two years despite solid growth and continued (well) above -target inflation. Second, as we argued recently, weak hiring trends are at the core of why household perceptions of the labor market -- and broader economy -- are historically downbeat despite strong growth (see “Downbeat labor sentiment reflects less dynamism”). We, therefore, see the potential resolution of this divergence as a critical determinant of the Fed outlook and possibly the midterm election outcome. If hiring trends converge towards growth, the labor market will strengthen, and the Fed will be unlikely to cut until inflation has demonstrated clearer evidence of moving back towards 2%. records.text: FX Views: Gold's enduring shine Themistoklis Fiotakis(i) Barclays, UK | Lefteris Farmakis(i) Barclays, UK Technically stretched, overvalued, but not a bubble Price action in gold has been nothing short of remarkable since the start of the year. At the end of 2025 gold was sitting at c. $4300. Within 25 days, it almost hit $5600, only to retrace to around $4900 within the space of two days. According to nearly all standard metrics gold screens as technically stretched (eg option skews, RSI) or over-positioned. The sharp turnaround last week suggests this is indeed the case. The more interesting question, however, is whether gold is fundamentally mispriced – a bubble that is a by-product of exuberance and is bound to unwind to meaningfully lower levels. Here the answer is more nuanced. We argue that while substantially overvalued in our estimates at present, it is no bubble. By contrast, there remain positive reasons why gold can sustain a sizable - though potentially less extreme - premium for a while, notwithstanding interim volatility. According to our model, gold's fair value is just under $4000 (Figure 7 - for more details see Of gold and safe havens). Thus, gold is just over 20% overvalued at the moment on our estimates, up from around 15% at the start of the year (and down from a peak of 40% only a few days ago). In the Bank's central projections, a forward-looking Taylor rule (something Governor Bailey ascribed to in the November forecast update), had Bank Rate slowing to 3.1% by the end of the year. In a scenario of inflation persistence, Bank Rate is estimated to drop to 3.2% under the forward-looking Taylor rule. And in a weak demand scenario, Bank Rate is expected to drop to as low as 2.7% (using the same policy rule). Overall, even looking at the stickier 'optimal policy paths' estimated by Bank staff, Bank Rate is estimated to drop below current levels. The MPC's forward guidance is clear - Bank Rate will likely reduce further in the coming months/quarters. Beyond the more finely balanced split vote (5-4), the MPC's tone was clear: more rate cuts are coming – notwithstanding some uncertainty around the timing of future rate cuts. Looking at the centrists, the case for further rate cuts remains - or indeed has strengthened. This means that bills have borne the brunt of the growing deficit, as government shortfalls have been slightly better than expected in the face of stronger economic activity and tariff revenue contributions. Furthermore, the impact of growing spending in the face of last year’s OBBB legislation was fairly muted in 2025, but is expected to ramp this year, with larger tax refunds in the coming months the start of widening deficits. There are of course risks to a strategy that is overly reliant on bill issuance. The refinance risk on the short end is well documented in the emerging markets, with reliance on external investors a somewhat relevant consideration in the UST market. We are nonetheless not overly concerned with a failed auction, instead, simply pointing out that Bessent and the Administration are acutely aware of the cost at the long end of the curve. What is the Birth-Death model and why does BLS use it? The Establishment survey applies a Birth-Death model adjustment to account for net employment changes from new business formations (births) and closures (deaths) that are not yet captured in the monthly sample in the CES based Establishment survey for payrolls. This is because new firms enter the survey with a lag and failing firms can drop out quickly. This is intended to prevent undercounting in expansions and overcounting in downturns. To compensate for this unavoidable lag, the BLS adjusts its monthly employment estimates using a two-part procedure: first, it imputes continued employment to firms that have disappeared from the sample (offsetting missing job gains from births), and second, it applies a time series model trained on five years of historical QCEW microdata to estimate the residual net effect of business openings and closings. The Cross-Border Equity Flow Indicator (xbEFI) measures the purchases and sales of equities by institutional investors, and is produced on a daily basis with a two day publication lag. The Cross -Border EFI focuses on trades by investors with base currencies that differ from a stock’s settlement currency. The indicator also includes transactions where the investor’s base currency is the same as the currency in which the trade is settled, and the settlement currency is different from that of the stock’s country of incorporation. An example of such a trade would be the purchase of a Dutch company’s American Depositary Receipts by a U.S. dollar-based fund. The Sovereign Bond Flow Indicator (SBFI) measures the purchases and sales of domestic and foreign sovereign bonds by institutional investors across countries and in regional aggregates and is available in unweighted and duration -weighted forms. We use unweighted flows in this document to capture the most relevant variable for a currency view. The SBFI is updated daily with a two-day publication lag. We use cross-border sovereign bond flows where available and total sovereign bond flows for all other countries.

We close the trade ideas we initiated in FX: Re-entering long KRW, funded with USD and CNH on 21 January for a combined profit of USD93k. USDKRW has jumped again alongside the reversal trend in the USD, as the market has recognized Kevin Warsh – the incoming Fed chairman – as a credible candidate who could ease concern on Fed independence, as well as global investors’ trust on the USD (see Sunday Tea with BNPP: The art of Warsh, dated 1 February). Since the market has taken us through our trailed stops, we close the trade ideas now (see FX: Trail stop and extend target on KRW longs, dated 28 January), locking in gains of 1% and 0.86% for USDKRW and CNHKRW respectively (close out levels in USDKRW: 1445, USDCNH: 6.8818, 10:01 GMT+8). We are keen to re-engage KRW long positions at better levels, as our medium-term bullish view on the KRW remains intact, considering upcoming WGBI inclusion inflows, government efforts to channel long -term capital into South Korean equities, robust fundamentals for the Kospi, and a chip super-cycle (see FX: Fading KRW weakness, sell USDKRW 6m NDF, dated 21 November 2025). The ceiling for the USDJPY would decline from around ¥160/$ to about ¥157.5/$, while the fall to some ¥150/$ could also be brought forward (we expect a shift to a core range centering on ¥152.5/$–¥157.5/$). The equity market is likely to react positively to the stabilization of the JPY and an end to the rise in Japanese interest rates in this case. Consequently, this should provide support to the strong gains by equities that, as we note above, are expected by our Japan Equity Strategy Team. When the equity market rises, normally there is likely to be JPY-selling hedging by a range of investors both in Japan and overseas, putting upward pressure on the USDJPY. However, similar to the divergence between Japanese equities and the USDJPY over the past year, the sensitivity of each to the other is weakening (Figure 4). Given also the latent upside pressure on the JPY due to the recent increase in Japanese bond yields, we do not think gains by Japanese equities will directly translate into ongoing depreciation in the JPY. records.text: residual seasonality will provide a significant boost to January payrolls in 2026. Will the HH survey data also be revised in the Jan report? The BLS typically incorporates new population estimates into the Household survey with the January jobs report. This year, however, the agency has announced that the updated population controls will instead be introduced with the February jobs report which will be released in March, likely reflecting delays stemming from last year’s shutdown. These revisions will apply only on a go forward basis, which means there will be level shifts in measures such as household employment, unemployment, and the labor force in February. As a result, monthly changes in these variables for February should be interpreted with caution. We expect the population update to produce downward revisions. Census Bureau estimates for July 2024 to July 2025 show U.S. population growth running at roughly half the prior year’s pace due to lower net migration. So, we expect a reduction in the labor force and household employment & unemployment levels in February.

Our models interpret the sell-off as a normalization of the previously inflated gold and silver valuations. In contrast, the drop in platinum’s spot price looks excessive, positioning the metal as the strongest candidate for a near-term rebound. Our ComFA and MarFA Macro models flag an undervaluation of –2.7 and –2.5 z-scores, respectively (Figures 1 and 2). Within our commodity model, the spot decline has outpaced the fair-value estimation, driven primarily by a stronger USD and a rising Fed financial stress index. Additionally, the Mann-Kendall test identifies an uptrend, reinforcing the case for a long trade. Fundamentally, platinum remains attractive because we anticipate a supply deficit extending into 2026, following the shortfall experienced in 2025. Tightening emissions standards and a slower-than-expected uptake of electric vehicles represent the principal demand catalysts. records.text: terogeneous across industries: When metal prices rise, the immediate effect is seen in producer price indices for industries directly related to metal manufacturing, and with a lag for the downstream industries that rely on metal inputs. Indeed, we find that the average lag in PPI prices to a metal price shock is about eight months. In addition, the correlation also varies, understandably so, given different metal exposures across industries (see heatmap in Figure 6). The lag structure may also have something to do with inventories and contracts, in that manufacturers tend to sign contracts to purchase inputs beforehand. • Cost-sharing and pricing power: Whether higher producer prices translate to higher consumer prices depends on how much of those cost pressures producers choose to pass onto consumers. If they instead decide to absorb into margins, the passthrough from PPI to CPI will likely be less than complete. In reality, passthrough tends to be less than proportional – empirical studies across many products find that a 10% increase in input costs leads to <10% increase in output prices on average, implying less than 100% passthrough2 . However, Sangani (2024) finds while the passthrough seems less than complete in percentage terms, it is complete in level terms, i.e., a $1/unit increase in commodity costs leads to $1/unit higher downstream prices. • Demand versus supply-side factors: Many metal prices, such as copper, tend to be pro- cyclical. Job openings peaked at 2.0 jobs per worker (about 12mn) in early 2022 (Figure 2). Labor market churn little changed, with hiring and separation rates matching once again The hiring and separation rates matched each other again in December, at 3.3%. In particular, the hiring rate ticked up 0.1pp in December, returning toward the middle of its 3.2-3.5% 12m range. The total level of hires increased to 5.293mn (+172k from November), with private-sector hiring increasing to 4.978mn (+152k). The overall separation rate edged up 0.1pp to 3.3% (Figure 3), reflecting modest increases in quits (+11k, to 3.204mn), layoffs and discharges (+61k, to 1.762mn), and other separations (+36k, to 285k). In all, the JOL TS release shows that hires minus separations amounted to 42k in December. Treasury and TBAC are monitoring Fed T-bill purchases and growing demand for bills in the private sector. Both TBAC charges presented cases to expand issuance in T-bills or front-end coupons. TBAC minutes also noted that the short and intermediate sectors of the UST curve were likely to experience the broadest growth. The post-refunding sell-off and our view for higher rates through H1 could make the May refunding a more significant inflection point for Treasury's objective to moderate long-end rates. Against this market backdrop, we think it would be in Treasury's best interest to lower the duration profile of its issuance. T-bill seasonality looks regular and predictable through H1: Treasury said it expects to maintain offering sizes of T-bill auctions at current levels into mid-March. Taking Monday's financing estimates into account, this should imply $260bn in bill issuance for Q1 and $242bn in bill paydowns through Q2. Treasury already issued $49bn in bills through January and expects to issue an additional ~$200bn over the next two months. This is to offset the typical February-March decline in TGA associated with tax refunds, which are likely to be larger this year due to the implementation of 2025's tax bill. records.text: US Economic Viewpoint | 05 February 2026 3 Given the wide array of factors impacting each of these updates, below we answer some frequently asked client questions on each topic. We also detail out our estimate for the expected size of the revisions, along with implications for the labor market and the Fed. FAQs: QCEW-based benchmark revisions What is the QCEW? Is it better than the payroll survey? The QCEW data represent approximately 95% of total employment and are compiled from state level unemployment insurance data that nearly all employers are required to file. This dataset is more accurate for estimating nonfarm payrolls than the Establishment survey, which samples about 120k businesses and government agencies (covering one-third of payroll employment) in the CES (Current Employment Statistics) survey. But the problem is the QCEW data are published with a lag of about five months, while the payroll data are published in a timelier manner at a monthly frequency. What is the annual QCEW based benchmark revision? Each year with the release of the January employment report, the Establishment survey data are benchmarked by the BLS to reflect more complete counts of employment from the QCEW. Hence in February of this year along with the release of the January employment report, the payroll data from April 2024 to December 2025 will be subject to a benchmark revision by the BLS. Imported cost shocks, post covid, and yen depreciation initiated the inflation cycle in the economy. The inflationary impulse is now led by du rable domestic forces – namely historically tight labor markets and sustained wage gains. The Bank of Japan’s (BoJ) gradual normalization has lifted short term rates, while long term yields have risen more sharply as markets reassess Japan’s new inflation regime. • State Street’s PriceStats signals were early in detecting an inflationary rise in Japan. Meanwhile, flows into selective EM r isk, from Brazilian equities to the TRY have remained firm. Economic data continues to be firm, especially export figures out from Asia. The global cycle has shown few signs of running out of steam and markets expect the Federal Reserve to remain in easing mode. As for the ZAR, historically the most volatile of EM currencies, its recent rise did not quite match the surge in South Africa’s terms of trade so it is unlikely to have become too expensive. We have faith in the global cycle and the Fed to both underpin risk and therefore made no changes to the portfolio this week by sticking with EM ex -Asia carry and relative value trades within EM Asia. Most of the time financial markets self-correct such divergences, but on rare occasions they require more direct actions from policy makers. These short- term risks will continue till Japanese bond and currency markets remain highly volatile and detached from value. records.text: FOCUS F O C U S 04/02/2026 1 “T-bill and chill” is alive … but the affordability push needed more: At the November refunding, the US Treasury surprised investors by saying it was “preliminarily considering” an increase in coupon sizes. The Treasury clarified that guidance this month by noting that an increase in coupons would be linked to “trends in structural demand” while citing “growing demand for bills” in the same breath. There were also suggestions from the TBAC to increase T-bill issuance and focus on raising coupon supply in shorter tenors and intermediate maturities. All of the above reinforces our structural view that the Treasury is likely to focus any incremental financing needs in bills (and front-end coupons), i.e. ”T-bill and chill”. While the Treasury discussion does reinforce our view, we acknowledge that the discussion was not overt enough for long-end swap spreads to widen (see US rates: Two chances, one opportunity, dated 29 January). We maintain long 30y spreads for now, given the focus on affordability and the recent weakness, and think they remain a good hedge to our 1s30s swap steepener view. By contrast, oil markets have seen supply disruptions ease quite significantly over the past few years and the OPEC+ pivot last year exacerbated the effect of a one-time level shift in demand due to COVID-19. Despite electrification of transport, oil demand remains quite resilient, in our view, and capacity constraints are a big theme in oil markets too. We think the cost of replacement for oil, at mid-cycle levels of activity, is likely above $80/b for Brent, much higher than current prices. The effect of business births and deaths is fully visible in the QCEW data. The BLS runs a simulation, computing QCEW-based payroll estimates using the continuing businesses and the same assumption about births offsetting deaths. It then compares the QCEW simulation to their full estimate of payrolls from QCEW. The difference between the two shows excess employment changes due to births/death---the historical errors from the payrolls estimate's method of imputing business births. BLS uses an ARIMA process on those past errors, to estimate the excess net business births and deaths in payrolls since the most recent (QCEW-based) benchmarking of payrolls. Thus the published birth-death adjustment does not reflect all of the employment due to business establishment openings and closings. Rather, it reflects the excess: those not covered by the assumption that business nonresponses and zeros are offset by business births. The net birth-death adjustment has lessened benchmark revisions The method has been somewhat effective, lessening the size of benchmark revisions over the past 20 years. It’s imperfect – benchmark revisions have been large – but better than the alternatives.
