Demand for bonds is weak: India's insurance industry growth has slowed down to around 6% y/y from double- digit growth in the last few years, due to weak economic momentum and regulatory changes. India's Employees' Provident Fund Organisation is also decreasing its bond holdings and increasing its investments in equities to boost the overall return of the fund, thereby reducing the demand for bonds from this industry. Meanwhile, the demand from banks has also fallen due to a pickup in credit growth and less demand from the held-to-maturity (HTM) book. Previously, banks were permitted to shift investments to and from the HTM book once a year at the beginning of the accounting year. However, such transfers are now tightly regulated and restricted to exceptional circumstances, which has further reduced demand for bonds from banks. Finally, foreign investors remain on the sidelines, as the rate-cutting cycle is probably over. Combined with high taxes and elevated FX-hedging costs, this leaves minimal potential returns for them. Risk of hawkish RBI meeting: At the previous RBI meeting, the central bank cut policy rate by 25bp and maintained a neutral stance. And despite what should be near-ideal conditions today—policy rates around neutral and a steep yield curve—banks are still struggling to grow their loan books, with corporate and household lending stuck at roughly 2%. The latest Lending Officer Survey confirms that demand for corporate and consumer credit remains subdued (mortgages are holding up but slowing). Taken together, this points to weaker profitability ahead for banks—and raises broader concerns about Europe’s economic outlook. At a minimum, it points to riskier concentration in eps generation, the kind of risk that has a habit of surprising market participants. Weak lending growth has reduced the share of loans on balance sheets, pushing them to rely increasingly on non-interest income. The latest figures show non -interest income accounts for 43% of total revenues —the highest since 2018. While this looks supportive on the surface, current market conditions are unusually favourable for fee generation: ample volatility for trading desks, elevated asset prices for wealth and asset management, and still-reasonable funding costs for underwriting. We doubt these tailwinds will persist. The recent experience in the US—where banks were punished for an overreliance on fee income as costs rose—serves as a warning. Revisions of roughly 800k, especially if focused in 2H24 are unlikely to materially shift Fed policy as they broadly match what policymakers already expect. In recent years, state government issuances (SDLs) have been on the rise (Figure 3). In this budget, the tax share for states has been maintained at 41% for 2026-31, despite requests from numerous states to increase it to 50%. Without a substantial increase in tax revenue, this means that states will continue to face an increased burden of issuance, contributing to a heavy bond supply this year. The gross bond supply for FY26/27 for the center and states will cross INR31trn this year, in our view. Demand for bonds is weak: The demand side of the bonds is already weak this year. India's insurance industry growth has slowed down to around 6% year- over-year from double-digit numbers in the last few years, due to weak economic momentum and regulatory changes. India's Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) is also decreasing its bond holdings and increasing its investments in equities to boost the overall return of the fund. This has reduced the demand for bonds from this industry. The demand from banks has also reduced for bonds due to a pickup in credit growth and less demand for the Held to Maturity (HTM) book. Whatever one might make of Kevin Warsh as Chairman-elect of the Federal Reserve, it is hard to envisage the next few months passing as smoothly as rate volatility markets imply. If his past tone is any guide, he seems more likely to shoot from the hip than his predecessors, similar to the man who chose him, opening up the potential for more contentious dissent within the committee. His past commentary suggests he is not a big fan of the expectations-management (and volatility suppressing) procedures of forward guidance, or the continual stream of speeches and media appearances made by the regional presidents. And, if one had to guess at the path he will stake out in his opening months as Chairman, it would run contrary to his hawkish public image and favor more easing than is priced by rate markets and foreseen by his future co-workers. He wouldn’t have been picked otherwise. So it is with some curiosity that we note the most Fed -sensitive portions of the interest rate volatility surface as having little reaction to last week’s announcements or volatility in other markets (Figure 3). The skew of 3m2y swaptions, the spread of 50bps out-of-the-money receivers versus payers, has not shifted: markets expect the easing cycle to continue, but do not see it becoming more aggressive (nor, of course, do they see any risk of it ending or reversing). records.text: AI impact the neutral rate?, November 20, 2017 - we noted the stronger productivity associated with a widespread use of AI can put sharp upward pressure on the neutral rate over time. Additionally, we noted that Fed policymakers will also be attentive to the labor market if labor slack increases due to worker replacement or augmentation from AI. And in this case, even when the neutral rate is perceived to be higher, the Fed could cut rates to support the employment side of its mandate. We see two scenarios that US rates market can price: Scenario 1: The AI continued boom scenario: a twist steepener? In this scenario, one can assume that AI investment continues unabated into 2026, propping growth and productivity, and raising the perceived neutral rate, while also negatively affects parts of labor market. In this scenario we could see the market price a higher long term neutral, and high issuance (to fund AI projects) in the long-end – alongside a dovish Fed accounting for the Fed’s recent imbalanced reaction function - adding a bear or twist steepening risk to the curve. Higher neutral rates and increased issuance keeps long-end yields high: In the AI boom scenario, we expect the long-end of the UST curve to start baking in two factors (1) a higher neutral rate in long end forwards, amid a perceived productivity boom, as we noted above, and (2) continued increased in long-term issuance to finance AI investments, adding duration to the market, and raising term premiums. records.text: M Idea 4 Republicans. In other words, if significantly cutting spending is not achievable, nominal growth is the only way out. Regular readers of our research should be well versed in our views that the current period looks very much like the post-WWII era from an economic standpoint, the last time debt/ GDP was so high. The path out required strong real and nominal growth for a decade-plus to stabilize financial metrics. “Running it hot” is now a popular phrase, but we were early to adopt this view with our ”hotter but shorter” framework in early 2021. This came on the back of our focus on “helicopter money” and fiscal dominance at the lows of the COVID pandemic in April of 2020. What has transpired since then was quite predictable, in our view—higher inflation and nominal GDP growth with more volatile economic data than we saw during the prior 30 years. LLC US Daily: The Growing Challenge of Housing Affordability 2 February 2026 | 9:12AM EST The cost of living has become a major political theme in recent years. This might n seem surprising at first because real disposable income, both in aggregate and for each income quintile, returned a while ago to roughly its pre-pandemic trend. But housing, particularly owner-occupied housing, continues to present a major affordability challenge, especially for low-income families. For renters, housing costs are high by historical standards. Rent currently n amounts to 32% of the average renter’s household income, somewhat above the 27% share in 2000. But it amounts to 55% of income for the bottom quintile and 40% for the second lowest quintile, each roughly 5pp higher than in 2000. For prospective homeowners, the affordability math is even more daunting. Both n the down payment-to-income and the mortgage-to-income ratios surged to 30-year highs in 2022 and have since remained elevated. For young married couples considering buying their first home, the average down payment is now 70% of their annual household income (vs. 58% in 2019 and 45% in 2000), and the first-year mortgage payment is about 25% (vs. 18% in 2019 and 20% in 2000). The left panel of Exhibit 5 shows that, even in 2000, the combined down payment and first-year mortgage costs for owner-occupied homes in the three largest metros—Los Angeles, San Francisco, and New York—had already reached 120% of household income, higher than the 65% average in smaller metros. Today, these large metros are even more expensive. First-time home buyers now need to spend almost two years of their household income on average for the down payment and first-year mortgage, significantly higher than the 80% share paid by households in the rest of the US outside of the largest cities. For households in the bottom income quintile, the cost of owning has risen substantially from 90% to over 160% in the past two decades, and for the second-lowest quintile it has risen from 60% to 100%. For households in the top income quintile, in contrast, the cost of owning has only increased from 40% to 60%. Shifting regulations, shifting risks: European insurers will see their interest-rate risk profiles reshuffled with the next wave of Solvency II (S2) reforms set to take effect in January 2027. Those reforms will replace the current Smith-Wilson (SW) extrapolation with the Alternative Method (AM), meaning that market rates beyond the 20-year point will now play some part in shaping the long end of the S2 discount curve. At first glance the shift may appear uneventful – the SW and AM curves are similar in today’s rate environment (Figure 1). However, we believe that the long-end extrapolation changes introduce important shifts in insurers’ key-point risk exposures across the curve. In this publication we elaborate on analysis in our August 2025 deep dive on the European insurance sector (see Revitalized inflows, regulatory shifts drive gentle uptick in EGB demand). What is changing? Under the current SW build method, the final point on the curve utilised in the extrapolation (known as the Last Liquid Point or LLP) is the 20y swap rate versus 6-month Euribor. amenities are predominantly owner-occupied (left, Exhibit 7), and the quality of these local public schools is also positively correlated with local home prices (right, Exhibit 7). As a result, for many households, the unaffordability of owner-occupied housing is more than just a cost of living problem. It also means higher barriers to building wealth and more limited access to education services, job opportunities in large and growing cities, and long-term social mobility. In our prior work, we highlighted that restrictive land use regulations are the primary driver of the housing shortage in the US. Large-scale reforms that relax local land use regulations can help to boost housing supply and alleviate the affordability crisis. However, land use regulations in the US are set by local communities, and changing them will likely involve complex legal and legislative processes. In the near term, providing subsidies to encourage the construction of affordable housing and implementing policy programs that help to lower financing costs for first-time home buyers, especially low-income households, can also be viable policy options. Nevertheless, for these solutions to have a long-lasting impact, they must eventually be integrated with broader, more comprehensive reforms that ease the existing regulatory constraints on the overall supply of housing. The estimated short-term borrowings have also increased by INR1.3trn in this budget, adding upward pressure on short-term yields. In recent years, state government issuances have been on the rise (Figure 3). In this budget, the tax share for states has been maintained at 41% for 2026–31, despite requests from several states to increase it to 50%. Without a substantial increase in tax revenues, states will probably continue to face an increased issuance burden, contributing to a heavy bond supply this year. Overall, we estimate the gross bond supply for FY2026– 27 for the central government and states combined will exceed INR31trn this year (Figure 3). records.text: Noel Dixon 02 February 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General RBA Preview: Insurance Hike December headline CPI came in uncomfortably high for the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), exceeding both consensus forecast and the RBA’s own estimates from its November monetary policy report (MPR). Additionally, Q4 trimmed mean inflation – the RBA’s preferred gauge of underlying inflation – also reached its highest level in five quarters, significantly exceeding the RBA’s target range. Coupled with a tight labour market, this suggests that the RBA’s policy stance may not be restrictive enough. Therefore, we expect the RBA will likely deliver a 25bps insurance hike at its 3 February meeting. However, given the recent volatility in labour market data, the RBA will probably be cautious about indicating a series of hikes. Meanwhile, the February MPR is likely to show an adjustment higher for both the growth and inflation outlook. Overall, the factors mentioned above, combined with a boost from rising metals demand, keep us positive on the AUD in the medium- term. Since its last December meeting, inflation has moved even further away from the RBA’s target range. PriceStats is showing a persistent trend creeping above its 10yr average (Figure 1). December CPI came in at 3.8% yoy, exceeding both consensus forecasts and the RBA’s own forecast in its November MPR. The move in inflation was quite broad based (Figure 2). By contrast, unit carbon costs are expected to peak later in the decade, but still below 1%. Carbon costs were comparatively muted during the energy crisis despite high EUA prices because free allocations and indirect cost compensation dampened the effective burden. However, they are expected to rise later in the decade reflecting declining free allocation under Phase IV and CBAM and higher assumed EUAs. As energy costs fade, carbon costs increasingly drive the unit-cost profile. This is visible both at the headline industry level and across single sectors, with unit carbon costs accelerating as free allocation declines and EUA prices rise. Importantly, this increase is policy-driven rather than energy-driven, marking a structural shift in cost composition. The Oil & Gas sector stands out as the sector with by far the highest unit carbon costs throughout the whole horizon. Even historically, the Oil & Gas sector already carries materially higher unit carbon costs than other sectors. Into the late 2020s, its unit carbon cost rises sharply and becomes dominant. records.text: closings. Why did BLS change the Birth-Death model methodology? Post pandemic business dynamics produced unusually large forecast errors, as firm creation and closures shifted sharply. To improve accuracy, the BLS temporarily adjusted the model from April through October 2024 by incorporating current sample-based employment growth, making the adjustment more responsive to current labor market conditions. With the release of the December 2025 jobs report, the BLS has announced that this current sample informed approach will be adopted permanently starting with the January 2026 employment report. What is our estimate for the Birth-Death model revision? Business formation has cooled materially from post pandemic highs, while closures and survival rates have risen amid tighter financial conditions and slower growth. The historically trained model likely overstates the job gains from net new businesses. Indeed, as seen in Exhibit 4, net establishment birth-death adjustment from the BLS’s Birth-Death model, despite slowing down in the last year continues to be above pre- pandemic levels. However, data on firm openings and closures from the Business Employment Dynamics (BED) Survey suggest that net establishment change is now running below its pre-pandemic levels. Using real time survey signals as part of the new methodology should lower the Birth- Death model contribution to job gains, particularly in a cooling labor market. The market added around 10bp to March, with c. 45bp priced in by December (Exhibit 1). Back in November, we were highlighting that February-June 2026 spread in MPC-dated Sonia was too flat relative to our expectations. Today’s price action brought the front- end curve much closer to our own expectations, and we turned neutral on the spread at the February 2026 MPC‑dated Sonia expiry (see UK Rates Alpha, 5 February). With 33bp priced in by June and 45bp by year‑end, and with some risk of cuts being delayed, we judge 2026 Bank Rate‑cut pricing to be much fairer. We also note that market pricing is increasingly at odds with our view that the Bank will remain on hold throughout 2027 (Exhibit 2). Easing bias was intact at today’s meeting and Governor Bailey noted that hikes were not discussed. Given the lag in disinflation and easing cycle in the UK, we think the bar for BoE to hike in 2027 is still very high. At present, we continue to think that the FOMC will be more focused on incoming inflation prints, after it cut rates three times last year amid labor market concerns. We expect the FOMC to cut rates 25bp at the June and December meetings after it sees signs that inflationary pressures have diminished. After that, the committee will likely keep an eye on labor market prints to detect any signs of deterioration conditions. According to the Beveridge curve, a drop in labor demand (as measured by the job opening rate) would likely come at the cost of larger increases in the unemployment rate than occurred earlier in the expansion. However, reductions in immigration flows are likely to moderate labor supply growth, muting the effect on the unemployment rate. These risks should keep the Fed attentive to movements of the unemployment rate and to job openings per unemployed as measures of slack. 5 February 2026 2 Barclays | US Economics

Although the pair has recently rallied — now about 1.3 z - scores above our MarFa fair value — the Sol is fundamentally supported by record - high terms of trade, driven by elevated copper and gold prices, and could also benefit from seasonal liquidity needs surrounding the upcoming corporate tax season. Strong terms of trade supports PEN: The PEN stands to gain from still - elevated copper and gold prices and Peru’s strong metal - export profile. Since November 2025, copper and gold have each jumped roughly 20 %. Together they accounted for about 54% of Peru’s annual export value (USD49bn). Even a modest 10% increase in exports balances would add roughly USD5bn — about 1.5 % of GDP — to the current account, widening the trade surplus. Nevertheless, the PEN has not yet fully priced in these strong metal prices. A comparable copper - gold rally in February – April 2024 saw the USDPEN depreciate about 5.2% despite a stronger USD, suggesting that the PEN still has considerable upside potential over the next few months, as it has only modestly appreciated since November 2025. Tax season could give the PEN an extra lift: Local firms usually convert foreign - currency earnings into PEN to meet seasonal cash needs such as taxes and dividends, with most USD sales concentrated in March - April. Recently we (and many other forecasters) have been dialing up that optimism. Starting with the January payroll report, our view has been that less intense holiday season hiring will entail fewer-than-usual job cuts after the period. This should be reflected in stronger seasonally adjusted hiring in January. Our estimate for January nonfarm payrolls is a gain of 105k, and we expect a steady unemployment rate at 4.4% - with risks to an even lower unemployment rate. That payroll growth would be nearly double the requirement to maintain the unemployment rate (see US January jobs preview: Better days, dated 30 January). Recent data also poses some upside risk to our already above-consensus growth estimate for Q4 2025 (Figure 3). Momentum should continue in Q1 as households see record tax refunds in the wake of last year’s OBBBA. Another “upside surprise” for January core CPI? January core CPI has surprised to the upside versus Bloomberg consensus expectations in 14 of the last 15 years. Even recent February CPI prints have been strong. While we have sympathy for the argument that a rise in unemployment driven by AI could be structural, it is not clear that the Fed would interpret it that way too, especially under the imbalanced reaction function. For instance, NY Fed President Williams suggested that he doesn’t see AI changing the natural rate of unemployment – suggesting a weaker employment picture may be met with a dovish Fed response.
